finding: Board captions change from page to page: 'Board 1: Store Config' (p1) / 'Store & Ops Config' (p4) / 'Store & POS Config' (p5); 'Board 2: Products & Pricing' / 'Product & Catalog'; 'Board 5: Promotions & Channels' / 'Promotions & Comm.'.
why_it_matters: Board names are what the client signs off and what the build names its screens. Three names for one board is three entries in a backlog and an argument at UAT.

source: Inventory & Procurement, Retail and F&B board packs
where: frame badges - Inventory p5, Retail p1, F&B p2, F&B p6
finding: Frames are missing from four pages across three packs. The Inventory pack is the clear case and was verified directly: every page banner reads 'ALL 10 PAGES', and Board 5 renders frames 1-7, 9, 10 - nine screens where the banner promises ten, with no frame 8. Retail p1 (1-8, then 10), F&B p2 (7, 8, 10) and F&B p6 (6, 7, 8, 10) skip a badge the same way, though those packs carry no banner stating the expected count. why_it_matters: On the Inventory pack the pack itself says a screen is missing. A screen nobody can see is a screen nobody will build, estimate or test. Since a complete pack does carry exactly ten frames per board, the skipped badges in the Retail and F&B packs are most likely dropped screens too, not loose numbering.
raised_by: G8, G9, G10, verified by orchestrator

finding: Only the page header carries a frame badge; the other 14 panels are unnumbered.

finding: The recording was filed under 'F&B, Retail, Procurement & Inventory' but the session actually covered CRM, Marketing and CMS. The F&B workshop it was filed as remains outstanding.

finding: The file carries a .docx extension but its contents are plain Markdown text, not a Word document.

where: five of the seven board packs
finding: FB_Dashboard_Screens, Inventory_Procurement_Dashboard_Screens, Retail_Dashboard_Screens_Only, TICVAI_POS_Frontline_Dashboard_Screens_Reference and TICVAI_Resource_Management_All_Screens carry no text layer at all - each page is a single flat image.

finding: Neither specification carries a precise date - only 'September 2026' and 'AUGUST 2026'.
why_it_matters: Where a spec and a later meeting disagree, the undated spec cannot be shown to be the older document.
raised_by: G7

where: chart labels, legend values and small numerics throughout

Readers recorded the surrounding requirement and left the figure out rather than guess it.

finding: The left rail lists two boards numbered 6 and no board numbered 5: the highlighted entry 'Board 6 - Sourcing & PO' is the page whose own header reads 'BOARD 5: SOURCING & PURCHASE ORDER MANAGEMENT', and a second entry reads 'Board 6 - Receiving & GRN'. No page in the pack is a receiving or GRN board - the actual Board 6 page header reads 'BOARD 6: PROCUREMENT SPEND, SAVINGS & COMMERCIAL ANALYTICS'. Verified by reading the rail and all three page headers directly.

Receiving and GRN is not a detail - it is where stock enters the business and where a three-way match against the purchase order happens. Either a board was cut, or the rail is advertising a workflow nobody has designed.
raised_by: G9, verified by orchestrator

finding: The board title is printed 'ANALYTICS, GOVERNANCE & RESOURCE CONTIOL CENTER' - CONTROL is misspelled - and frame 4 carries the badge '00' instead of '04'.

action: Fix the title and the frame badge in the design source.

finding: Twenty-eight requirement IDs are each used by two different requirements. The worst block is 22.3.1-22.3.10, where rows 2901-2910 are case management (Case Creation, Case Classification, SLA Management, Case Audit Trail) and rows 2911-2920 are marketing journey automation (Visual Journey Builder, Event Trigger Engine, Conditional Logic & Decision Trees, Birthday & Anniversary Campaigns). Blocks 5.6, 8.1 and 5.5 collide likewise. Counted directly from the sheet.
why_it_matters: A traceability entry citing '22.3.1' is ambiguous between case creation and a journey builder - two unrelated capabilities. Every register that traces to a colliding ID is citing a row number in disguise, and at sign-off the client can reasonably read it either way.
raised_by: orchestrator, counted from the matrix
action: Renumber one side of each colliding block before traceability is agreed. The 22.3 block first - it is inside Marketing & CRM, which is where a scope argument will start.

where: domain 7 sub-domain 7.5 'Kitchen Display', and the real kitchen rows scattered across domains 4, 5 and 10
finding: All ten rows filed under 'Kitchen Display' are about something else: event table booking, ticket no-show handling, invitation campaigns for VIPs and sponsors, invitation quotas and URLs, event-entry QR validation, and multi-level approval for complimentary tickets. The actual kitchen-display requirements do exist, but none of them is in that sub-domain - they are 4.6.22 (link menu items to a kitchen printer/display), 4.6.33 (configurable kitchen routing to stations, printers and KDS screens), 4.8.3 (pass modifier data to the KDS), 5.1.11 (synchronise order status between POS and KDS in real time), 5.2.1 (work with kitchen displays, bump bar and kitchen printers), 5.2.2 (route KDS orders to devices by IP) and 10.1.1. Table reservation is the same story: the real rows are 4.9.13, 5.1.1 and 5.1.2, none in a sub-domain of that name.
why_it_matters: The capability is not missing - it is unfindable. Eight kitchen-display requirements are spread over four domains, under sub-domains labelled 'F&B POS - Core Ordering', 'Payment Methods' and 'Wallet', while the sub-domain actually called 'Kitchen Display' holds invitation management. Anyone scoping, estimating or testing the KDS by looking where its name is will find the wrong ten rows and miss the right eight.
raised_by: chunk01 adjudicator, then corrected and completed by the sighted re-check; verified by orchestrator
action: Re-file the kitchen rows under a real Kitchen Display sub-domain and move the invitation rows to events or marketing. Until then, do not scope KDS from the sub-domain name.

finding: Four sub-domain IDs each carry two different names: 5.4 is both 'Loyalty' and 'Unified Platform'; 5.5 is both 'Portfolio & Entitlement Management' and 'Portfolio Management'; 8.1 is both 'AI Configuration Assistant' and 'AI Governance & Explainability'; 8.3 is both 'AI Governance' and 'Fraud Detection'.
why_it_matters: Sub-domain is how the matrix is grouped for review and sign-off. Where one ID names two sub-domains, any count or filter by sub-domain silently merges them - including the counts quoted to the client.
raised_by: orchestrator, counted from the matrix
action: Give each sub-domain its own ID before the next count is published.

where: domain 6 Retail POS and domain 7 F&B POS - 229 rows
finding: The sub-domain labels in both POS domains do not describe their contents. All 78 Retail POS rows sit under one sub-domain called 'Wallet', but they are receipts, e-invoicing, nightly tender balancing, reporting and item lookup. In F&B POS, 7.1 'Retail POS' (62 rows) is user groups, rights, logins and password policy; 7.4 'Table Reservation' (52 rows) is the customer database - search, de-duplication, export and B2C/B2B segmentation; 7.5 'Kitchen Display' (10 rows) is invitation campaigns and event entry. Read directly from the sheet.
why_it_matters: The sub-domain is how the matrix is filtered, assigned to an owner and reviewed. Here it points the reader at the wrong subject for 229 rows - seven percent of the matrix. Two capabilities the boards assume, the Kitchen Display System and table reservations, appear to be covered because a sub-domain carries their name, while the rows underneath are about something else entirely. Anyone checking coverage by sub-domain name will conclude the opposite of the truth.
raised_by: orchestrator, read from the matrix
action: Re-label the sub-domains in domains 6 and 7 against their actual contents, then check whether Kitchen Display and Table Reservation have any requirements at all once the mislabelled rows are moved.

finding: No matrix requirement creates or configures a retail store or an F&B outlet. Searching all 3,184 rows for such an entity being created, set up, configured, onboarded or held as master data returns nothing; of the 25 rows containing 'store', most use it as a verb. The build, however, models it fully: contracts/spine/tenancy.yaml:2204 defines Outlet - 'a point of sale within a venue: a shop, a restaurant, a bar, a kiosk cluster' - with required code, name, venueId and kind, plus zone, stockLocationId, costCenterId, openingHours and isActive, a 409 on a duplicate code, and screens BO-728 to BO-732 behind it.
why_it_matters: This is traceability, not scope. The entity every retail and F&B board scopes by does exist and is properly specified - it is simply not obliged anywhere in the contract the client signed. The blind pass missed it for an instructive reason: it searched for 'store' and the project calls it an outlet. That one vocabulary mismatch produced around twenty false gaps on its own.
raised_by: chunk08 adjudicator, corrected by the sighted re-check; verified by orchestrator against tenancy.yaml
action: Add a matrix row obliging outlet master data so the build's Outlet has something to trace to, or record it as an agreed inheritance. Do not book it as missing scope - it is built.

source: three documents disagree: the matrix, the 18 August decision, and the Inventory & Procurement board pack
where: matrix 15.2.10-15.2.13, backlog BL-158, and INVPROC board page 2 (Warehouse Operations)
finding: The client decided against a warehouse execution layer at the 18 August workshop. The backlog records it as withdrawn scope in terms - BL-158, 'No warehouse execution layer - putaway, picking, packing, dispatch or warehouse tasks. Withdrawn - the client decided against a warehouse execution layer at the 18 August workshop.' The minutes of that workshop say the same: 'the team agreed NOT to implement every status.' But the matrix still requires four of them - 15.2.10 Picking Lists, 15.2.11 Picking Validation, 15.2.12 Partial Picking, 15.2.13 Packing Operations - and a board page was drawn for the withdrawn capability anyway: INVPROC page 2, Warehouse Operations, whose sixteen requirements have nothing to build against.
why_it_matters: A capability was withdrawn nine months before delivery and neither the contract nor the design caught up. The matrix still obliges it, so a tester will raise defects against it. A board page still shows it, so a client reviewing the designs will reasonably expect it. Sixteen extracted requirements sit on that page. This is the clearest instance in the whole exercise of a decision that did not propagate.
raised_by: chunk04 adjudicator, then confirmed by the sighted pass and partial-resolution chunk 24; BL-158 verified by orchestrator
action: Delete or explicitly except matrix rows 15.2.10-15.2.13, and withdraw INVPROC board page 2 or mark it out of scope. Then check whether any other withdrawn backlog item still has a matrix row and a board behind it - this will not be the only one.

source: POS Frontline board pack against the matrix
finding: The board sets a Group Booking Discount at a quantity of 10 or more. Matrix 3.6.28 reads 'It is possible for Groups of 15 people or more have dedicated Group prices.' Two different thresholds for the same concept.
why_it_matters: A threshold is testable, so this is a defect that will be found at UAT rather than in review. It is also the kind of number that has commercial consequences either way.
raised_by: chunk05 adjudicator, verified by orchestrator against both texts
action: Confirm whether the group threshold is 10 or 15, and correct the losing document.

source: POS Frontline board pack against the matrix
finding: The board provides a Payment Method Restriction that can block refunds in cash. Matrix 4.6.10 requires that the system 'be able to refund in different and multiple payment methods. For example, system to allow refunds in cash or original payment methods.'
why_it_matters: Less clear-cut than it first appears: the matrix requires the capability and the board restricts it by policy, which can coexist. It needs confirming rather than correcting - but if a tester reads 4.6.10 literally and the restriction is switched on, the system fails the test.
raised_by: chunk05 adjudicator, verified by orchestrator against both texts
action: Confirm that 4.6.10 is a capability requirement and that blocking cash refunds by configuration is acceptable against it.

where: matrix 6.1.78, against contracts/satellite/reporting.yaml and the dashboard specification
finding: The matrix does specify a reporting platform, in real detail, in a single 581-character row - 6.1.78. It obliges a self-service report builder, a dashboard designer, scheduled generation, report subscriptions, role-based report access, multi-site reporting, multi-language reporting in English and Arabic, exports to PDF/Excel/CSV/XML, API access, drill-down and drill-through, interactive dashboards, KPI scorecards, trend analysis, forecasting, comparative period analysis, a minimum seven years of reporting history with archival, and real-time and historical reporting. That row is filed under domain 6, sub-domain 'Wallet', inside Retail POS. What the matrix does not do anywhere is name a chart type: 'heat map' appears twice (21.5.24 seat selection, 1.2.71 resource utilisation) and every one of the six 'chart' mentions is 'Chart of Accounts'. The dashboard specification names 18 visual types; contracts/satellite/reporting.yaml:3257 commits to 8.
why_it_matters: The first read of this called the dashboard specification unpriced scope. That was wrong twice over. The build already commits to a chart catalogue, and the matrix already obliges most of the reporting platform - it is simply filed under Wallet in Retail POS, which is why three separate searches missed it. One row resolved about thirty-five requirements the blind pass had called gaps. The residual exposure is narrow and specific: the visual vocabulary. The client's spec asks for roughly ten visual types the contract does not commit to - waterfall, treemap, scatter, decomposition tree, funnel, ribbon, slicers and the rest.
raised_by: chunk24 adjudicator, counted and verified by orchestrator
action: Reconcile the visual-type lists only - 18 specified against 8 contracted - and decide what is priced. Do not raise the rest of the reporting platform as a gap; 6.1.78 covers it. And move 6.1.78 out of 'Retail POS / Wallet', because a reporting platform filed there will keep being missed.

where: matrix 1.4.4 against matrix 1.4.15, and against decisions recorded in two meetings
finding: Matrix 1.4.4 requires the system to 'propagate any changes made to the properties of a product to the already sold tickets as well.' Three things contradict it. Matrix 1.4.15, in the same sub-domain, requires products to be 'retired from sale without impacting previously sold tickets, memberships or reservations.' And the minutes record twice, independently, that a price or configuration change must never reprice or alter an already-sold ticket.
why_it_matters: This is the best-evidenced conflict in the set: one matrix row against another matrix row and against two separate recorded decisions. Retroactively repricing sold tickets is a commercial and legal exposure, not a display question, and 1.4.4 as written requires it. It is also the kind of row that passes review because it sounds like good data hygiene.
raised_by: chunk16 and chunk19 adjudicators, verified by orchestrator against the matrix
action: Correct or scope 1.4.4. The minutes and 1.4.15 agree with each other, so 1.4.4 is the outlier - state which product property changes may reach sold tickets, and confirm that price is not among them.

finding: 5.12.15 requires 'Revenue recognition on ticket sale payment.' 5.12.119 requires deferred revenue to move automatically to earned revenue, and 5.12.8 requires configurable revenue recognition rules. Recognising at the moment of sale and deferring until the visit are different accounting treatments of the same ticket.
why_it_matters: Revenue recognition timing is an audit-relevant accounting policy, not a preference. 5.12.8's configurability may reconcile the two, but only if someone states that 5.12.15 is one configurable option rather than the required behaviour. As written the matrix asks for both.
raised_by: chunk16 adjudicator, verified by orchestrator against the matrix
action: Confirm with finance whether ticket revenue is recognised at sale or at redemption, and mark 5.12.15 as an option if it is one.

source: method note - how this workbook was produced
where: the matching step between extracted requirements and the matrix
finding: Candidate matrix rows were proposed by lexical similarity, and that retrieval is weak on this pair of documents because both use the same vocabulary. Adjudicators repeatedly found that the true match scored near zero while a false friend ranked first - matrix 2.7.55 (per-partner dashboards with sales, commission and credit usage) scored 0.09 against four B2B rows it genuinely covers; 'Chart of Accounts' ranked top against a request for a chart; licence grace periods ranked top against a shift grace period; stock variance against cash variance; seat selection against workstation selection.
why_it_matters: It biases the result one way. A missed match becomes a Partial or an Absent, so the workbook understates coverage rather than overstating it. Adjudicators compensated by reusing correct matrix ids they had seen elsewhere in their own chunk, and each such row carries a note - but that only rescues a row when the right matrix row happened to surface somewhere nearby.
raised_by: chunk23 adjudicator and others, confirmed across chunks
action: Treat Absent as 'not evidenced here' rather than proven absent, and re-check any Absent row that matters commercially against the matrix by hand before quoting it to the client.

where: 7.6.8 against 7.6.15, both in the rental sub-domain
finding: 7.6.8 requires, at customer arrival: 'Scan voucher/ticket. Validate booking. Assign actual rental item. Scan serial number of rented equipment. Link equipment to reservation.' 7.6.15, fifteen rows later, opens 'The following are highly recommended and not currently covered in the proposed solution:' and its first item is 'Equipment assignment using QR/Barcode scanning.' One row requires the scan; the other says the scan is not covered.
why_it_matters: The matrix contradicts itself about whether a capability is in scope, in the same sub-domain, fifteen rows apart. 7.6.15 is also the only row in all 3,184 that describes what the solution does NOT do while still being counted as a requirement, so it inflates the requirement count by listing eight things nobody is committing to build.
raised_by: chunk20 adjudicator, verified by orchestrator against the matrix
action: Decide whether rental equipment scanning is in scope, then either delete 7.6.15 or move its eight items to a clearly marked exclusions list outside the requirement count.

finding: 5.9.2 requires the ability to do a 'blind' cashier close-out, where over-shorts are captured and recorded. 5.9.6 requires an alert when the expected till value and the counted value differ at end of shift. Neither row says who receives the alert.
why_it_matters: A blind close-out works precisely because the cashier cannot see the expected figure. If the 5.9.6 alert reaches the cashier, the control in 5.9.2 is defeated. The two rows are compatible only if the alert is scoped to a supervisor, and no row says so.
raised_by: chunk20 adjudicator, verified by orchestrator against the matrix
action: State that the variance alert goes to the supervisor, not the cashier, so the blind close-out survives implementation.

source: method note - how this workbook was produced
finding: The first pass showed adjudicators at most 260 characters of each matrix requirement. 213 of the 3,156 distinct matrix rows are longer than that, and they are disproportionately the rows that enumerate - 'Required Reports' followed by twenty report names, a capacity rule followed by the five levels it applies at. 1,000 adjudicated rows had seen at least one such truncated row and had been scored Partial or Absent. All 1,000 were re-judged against the full text.
why_it_matters: 52 verdicts of the 1,000 re-judged changed, 5.2 percent, and every single one moved towards more coverage - 31 Partial to Covered, 19 Absent to Partial, 2 Absent to Covered, none the other way. Concrete examples: matrix 3.2.7's hidden tail defines anti-passback re-entry timing and 'required exit before re-entry', which closed six rows the first pass called gaps; 1.1.10's tail defines Admission Capacity, which closed five capacity rows; 1.1.129's tail requires Round-Up Donation, which the first pass had reported as an unobliged donation type; 3.2.73's tail obliges operator switching of turnstile modes.
raised_by: orchestrator
action: None outstanding - the affected rows were re-judged and the workbook shows the corrected verdicts, with a 'Checked twice' column marking them. It is recorded here because it shows the direction of the residual error: this workbook understates coverage rather than overstating it.

where: matrix 8.5.26 against the catalogue import job state machine
finding: Matrix 8.5.26 reads 'System shall support rollback of pricing changes.' The build's own state machine says the opposite in terms: 'Partial application is recorded rather than rolled back - three thousand products half-created is a state somebody has to see to repair', and 'failed after committing is not a rollback. A partially applied catalogue is a real state.' Both read directly.
why_it_matters: This is the contract disagreeing with the design, not a gap. The build made a deliberate, reasoned decision - a half-applied import is visible and repairable rather than silently reversed - and the matrix obliges the behaviour that decision rejects. A tester holding 8.5.26 will raise it as a defect against a design that is working as intended.
raised_by: sighted shard 07, verified by orchestrator against both files
action: Either scope 8.5.26 to single pricing changes rather than bulk imports, or record the import-job decision as an agreed exception against it. This one will surface at UAT if left.

where: all 1,287 rows the blind pass called Absent or High-severity
finding: Every row the blind pass scored Absent, and every row it scored High severity, was re-checked by agents with full access to the whole matrix, the repository, the contracts and the screens. Roughly 84 percent of those verdicts changed, all upward. The blind pass was not judging badly - it was judging on five lexically retrieved candidate rows out of 3,184, and the matrix's structure defeats lexical retrieval.
why_it_matters: Three structural reasons the blind pass produced false gaps, all verified: long list rows (3.2.7 is 1,299 characters and enumerates anti-passback, required-exit-before-re-entry and entry quotas, none of which its opening sentence suggests); whole blocks never surfacing (the 80-row 11.1.x approval governance block, the 5.5.x entitlement block, all of domain 16 device management); and requirements filed under headings that describe something else (7.1.10 reads as a concurrent-logins row and carries the entire facility-capacity and channel-allocation specification in its details column).
raised_by: orchestrator
action: Use the sighted verdicts, not the blind ones, for any coverage figure. The blind pass is still valuable as an independent read of what the sources ask for - it just cannot be trusted on what the matrix contains.

where: the F&B depletion model and what it means for offline selling
finding: The minutes record that F&B recipe depletion is per-outlet configurable and typically runs end-of-day, the stated purpose being that F&B can keep selling while offline. The F&B contract takes the opposite position in its own text: its header says stock movement for recipe-linked items 'is real-time, so F&B is blocked offline where inventory is tracked', and placeOrder at line 4166 says an order 'containing a recipe-linked item is refused offline because stock depletes in real time'. Line 7217 repeats it: 'Stock-tracked items cannot be sold offline.'
why_it_matters: This is not a missing field, it is two incompatible operating models. One of them says a kitchen keeps taking orders when the network drops; the other says the till refuses them. Whichever is right, somebody is currently building against the other, and it touches ADR-0013. For a venue, the difference shows up as lost revenue on the first bad network day.
raised_by: partial-resolution chunk 06, verified by orchestrator against fnb.yaml
action: Settle the depletion model with the F&B lead: real-time depletion with no offline F&B, or deferred depletion with offline selling. Then correct whichever of the minutes or the contract is wrong.

source: contracts/ (all), against the Ticket Types board pack
where: validity windows, entitlement templates and time-slot rules
finding: Time semantics are undecided across the platform. A grep for 'daylight' or 'DST' across every contract returns nothing. Nothing states whether a validity boundary such as validTo or validTimeWindows.to is inclusive or exclusive. validTimeWindows is a pair of times of day, so an overnight window like 22:00 to 02:00 cannot be expressed. And daysOfWeek, validTimeWindows and blackoutDates carry no stated evaluation order, although the package states precedence explicitly everywhere else - approvals.yaml says 'Rules are ordered and the first match wins' and RefundPolicy.timeBands says 'most-specific first'.
why_it_matters: This is a correctness problem, not a documentation one. A ticket valid 'until 22:00' on the night the clocks change either admits a guest or refuses them depending on an answer nobody has given. An overnight validity window cannot be configured at all. And where two validity rules disagree, the system's behaviour is whatever the first implementer happened to code.
raised_by: partial-resolution chunk 19, verified by orchestrator with a repo-wide grep
action: Decide three things and write them into the catalogue contract: whether validity boundaries are inclusive, how DST transitions are handled for windows that span them, and the evaluation order of daysOfWeek, time windows and blackout dates. The precedence convention already used elsewhere in the package is the obvious model.

source: contracts/satellite/workforce.yaml and resources.yaml, against the Resource Management board pack
finding: A ratio such as 'one instructor per eight participants' cannot be expressed anywhere in the platform. Grepping every contract for capacityModel, staffRatio, onePer, participantRatio and minParticipants returns nothing. StaffingRules.minimumCover carries a flat minimum headcount per position code, and ResourceRequirement is a type and a quantity. The board pack's five-way Capacity Model selector, its participant min/max and its live sellable-capacity preview have no field and no operation behind them.
why_it_matters: The consequence is operational, not cosmetic. Sale-time capacity and roster-time cover have to evaluate the same expression, or a session sells more places than can be staffed - and nobody finds out until the guests arrive. Because the ratio has no home, the two sides are currently free to diverge by construction.
raised_by: partial-resolution chunk 18, verified by orchestrator with a repo-wide grep
action: Decide where a ratio lives and in what units, then make the sell path and the rostering path read the same expression. This is one decision that closes six board requirements.
